 More could lose SNAP benefits under proposed rule 
 About 6.3 million more people could lose eligibility if states can no longer automatically qualify TANF recipients
 Bill Wilson , Executive Editor at Supermarket News November 12, 2026
 1 Min Read Because TANF recipients can automatically qualify for SNAP at the state level, some states have used that instant qualification to expand SNAP benefits to people who might not otherwise qualify. Shutterstock Summarize this article The Trump administration has proposed a rule that could remove more people from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, according to multiple reports. 
 The rule would stop some beneficiaries of the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF, program from automatically qualifying for SNAP. The change could prevent about 6.3 million people from gaining SNAP eligibility by fiscal year 2029, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said. That number would add to the 5.5 million people who have lost SNAP benefits over the past year. 
 The public comment period for the proposed rule ends next month. 
 Because TANF recipients can automatically qualify for SNAP at the state level, some states have used that instant qualification to expand SNAP benefits to people who might not otherwise qualify. The proposed rule would end this practice. 
 A federal judge in Oregon ruled in September in favor of 22 states and the District of Columbia in a lawsuit seeking to preserve SNAP benefits for certain lawful permanent residents. 
 Related: USDA finally takes a stand on SNAP card skimming 
 The judge had previously issued an injunction in the case. Under that injunction, the states faced the risk of paying hundreds of millions of dollars in penalties for providing benefits to some lawful residents who are not U.S. citizens—also known as green card holders—including former refugees and people who had received asylum. 
 The Trump administration later reversed its position on eligibility for lawful permanent residents but continued to argue that states owed fines for missing a "grace period" that had effectively expired before the administration finished issuing guidance on the changes, according to Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who led the suit.
